brief.spec: Return a document only to a session from the document tenant. Request tenant filters are untrusted.
brief.context: Session identity is verified upstream. find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping; request parameters come directly from the URL.

expected.criterion: A caller can supply another tenant in the request and read its row because ownership is compared with untrusted request data instead of the authenticated session.

raw.title: Tenant check now trusts request.tenant from the URL instead of session.tenant, so any caller can read documents from other tenants
raw.evidence: The spec says to return a document only to a session from the document's tenant, and it says request tenant filters are untrusted. The context says find(id) is a global lookup with no tenant scoping and that request parameters come straight from the URL. The before code compared row.tenant === session.tenant. The after code compares row.tenant === request.tenant. Because the caller controls both request.id and request.tenant, they can set tenant to match any document's tenant and get that document back. This is a cross-tenant data leak, and the verified session identity is no longer used in the check.

raw.title: Tenant authorization check now trusts the request's tenant parameter instead of the verified session tenant

This breaks the spec: return a document only to a session from the document's tenant, and treat request tenant filters as untrusted. It is a cross-tenant IDOR/broken access control.
raw.location: module.js:read, line 3 (`return row && row.tenant === request.tenant ? row : null;`)

brief.spec: Add displayName to the response while supporting installed clients that still read name. All consumers must keep rendering a label.
brief.context: Mobile releases remain active for 90 days. Legacy code calls payload.name.toUpperCase(); the new web client reads payload.displayName.
brief.before: function response(row) { return {id:row.id, name:row.name, displayName:row.name}; }

expected.criterion: Removing name breaks still-supported installed clients that dereference payload.name; keep the old field until those consumers have migrated.

raw.title: Removing `name` from the response breaks installed mobile clients that still use it
raw.evidence: The spec says to add displayName while still supporting installed clients that read `name`, and says every consumer must keep rendering a label. Mobile releases stay active for 90 days, and legacy code calls payload.name.toUpperCase(). Before the change, the response returned {id, name, displayName}. After it, the response returns only {id, displayName}. On older clients payload.name is now undefined, so payload.name.toUpperCase() throws a TypeError and no label renders. Fix: keep `name: row.name` next to `displayName` until the 90-day window has passed with no remaining legacy readers, then remove it in a planned deprecation.

raw.title: Removing `name` breaks installed mobile clients that still read payload.name
raw.evidence: The spec requires support for installed clients that still read `name`, and says every consumer must keep rendering a label. The after version returns only {id, displayName}, so payload.name is undefined and calling .toUpperCase() on it throws a TypeError in legacy clients. That breaks the contract and the user-facing UI. Fix: keep `name: row.name` next to `displayName` until the 90-day legacy window has passed.

raw.title: No test covers the backward-compatible response shape
raw.evidence: The change includes no test that checks the response has both `name` and `displayName`. A contract test like that would have caught this removal. Add a test asserting response(row).name === row.name and response(row).displayName === row.name.

brief.spec: A retried delivery of the same event must not create a second charge, including after a worker restarts.
brief.context: charge(key) is the provider idempotency API: equal keys return the existing charge. A retry uses the same event.id but receives a new attemptId.
brief.before: function deliver(event, attemptId, charge) { return charge(event.id); }
brief.after: function deliver(event, attemptId, charge) { return charge(attemptId); }

expected.criterion: Using the per-attempt ID as the payment idempotency key creates another charge on a retry of the same event; the key must be stable for the logical payment.

raw.title: Retries use a new idempotency key and can create duplicate charges
raw.evidence: The change passes attemptId instead of event.id to charge(). Retries retain event.id but receive a new attemptId, so the provider no longer returns the existing charge. This violates the requirement to avoid duplicate charges on retries, including after worker restarts. Use event.id as the key.

raw.title: Retries use a new idempotency key and can create duplicate charges
raw.evidence: A retry preserves event.id but receives a new attemptId. Changing charge(event.id) to charge(attemptId) gives the provider a different idempotency key on every attempt, allowing a second charge for the same event, including after a worker restart. Use event.id to preserve the required deduplication.

triage.title: Retries can create duplicate charges
triage.evidence: Changing charge(event.id) to charge(attemptId) replaces the stable event key with a new key on each retry. Provider idempotency therefore no longer prevents a second charge for the same event, violating the retry contract, including after worker restarts. Merged sources: Operability and Staff engineer.

raw.title: Idempotency key changed from event.id to attemptId, so retries create duplicate charges
raw.evidence: The context says charge(key) only deduplicates when the keys are equal, and that a retry keeps the same event.id but gets a new attemptId. The 'after' code calls charge(attemptId), so every retry, including one after a worker restart, sends a new key and creates a second charge. This breaks the spec ('A retried delivery of the same event must not create a second charge'). The 'before' code, charge(event.id), met it. On-call also loses the ability to link duplicate charges back to a single event, because the provider key no longer contains event.id. Remediation would mean finding and refunding duplicates by hand.

brief.context: fs is an in-memory node map. A directory node may hold user-created content. Assignment replaces the entire node; no caller backup exists.

raw.title: Conflict guard removed: real files/directories at target are deleted and overwritten
raw.evidence: The before code had `if(fs[target] && fs[target].kind!=='link') return false;`. The after code runs `delete fs[target]; fs[target]={kind:'link',...}; return true;` with no check. Under the spec, real directories and files must be kept and the function must return false. The context says a directory node may hold user content, assignment replaces the whole node, and callers have no backup. So this change silently and permanently loses user data, and it breaks the return-false contract because it always returns true.

It also breaks the return-false contract: the only exit path is now `return true`, so callers can't detect conflicts. The spec says a human-only tool passes validation only if policy.allow_implicit_invocation is boolean false at the document root. The new code, `Object.values(config).some(section => section?.allow_implicit_invocation===false)`, returns true if any top-level value has that flag set to false. The loader reads only config.policy.allow_implicit_invocation, and when policy is missing it allows implicit invocation. Two examples show the break. `{metadata:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}` with no policy passes validation, but the loader still allows implicit invocation. `{policy:{allow_implicit_invocation:true}, other:{allow_implicit_invocation:false}}` also passes, while the loader honors policy:true. In both cases a tool marked human-only can be invoked implicitly, so the check fails open. This also breaks the validator/loader contract, which was the Data & contracts finding. The old code, `config.policy?.allow_implicit_invocation===false`, checked the path the spec requires.

brief.spec: Readers must handle legacy title records and newer label records. Introducing label must keep writes readable by consumers of title while the migration remains open.
brief.context: Existing records always have a nonempty title. Migrated records may have a nonempty label as well. Version-one consumers read title; version-two consumers prefer label.
brief.before:
function write(text) { return {title:text}; }
function read(row) { return row.title; }
brief.after:
function write(text) { return {title:text,label:text}; }
function read(row) { return row.label ?? row.title; }

raw.title: No tests cover the new dual-write and label-first read fallback
raw.evidence: The change makes write() return {title:text,label:text} and read() return row.label ?? row.title, but adds no tests. Four cases are untested: a legacy row with title only, which reads title; a migrated row with label and title, which reads label; written rows keeping title for version-one consumers; and a row whose label is null or undefined, which falls back to title. Tests for these would protect the readability promise the spec requires while the migration is open.

brief.spec: Closing the dialog with Escape must restore focus to the same control that opened it.
brief.context: open is called with the currently focused trigger. The renderer unmounts the dialog when state.open is false. trigger.focus() is the available way to restore focus.

expected.criterion: The Escape close path unmounts the dialog without restoring focus to its opener, so keyboard users lose their place in the screen.

raw.title: Escape no longer restores focus to the opening trigger
raw.evidence: Spec: "Closing the dialog with Escape must restore focus to the same control that opened it." The 'before' onKey sets state.open=false and then calls state.trigger.focus(). The 'after' onKey only sets state.open=false and drops the trigger.focus() call. The context says trigger.focus() is the available way to restore focus and that the renderer unmounts the dialog when state.open is false, so after this change focus is left on the removed dialog element and falls back to document body. Keyboard and screen-reader users lose their position in the page after closing the dialog, which breaks the stated contract.
raw.location: module.js, onKey(state,event) (after version), the line after state.open=false where state.trigger.focus() was removed

raw.title: Escape no longer restores focus to the opening control
raw.evidence: The change removes `state.trigger.focus()` from the Escape branch of `onKey`. It now only sets `state.open=false`. The renderer unmounts the dialog when `state.open` is false, so focus is lost, probably falling back to `body`. The spec requires focus to return to the same control that opened the dialog. `open` still stores `trigger`, so the stored value is now unused.

In the after version, it only runs `state.open=false;`. The context says the renderer unmounts the dialog when state.open is false, and that trigger.focus() is the available way to restore focus. brief.spec: Archive must act on the row selected by the user, including when the list is filtered or reordered after selection.
brief.context: select stores selection in parent state. Filter and sort replace rows but preserve selection. Every row has an immutable unique id; archive is the persistence callback.
brief.before:
function select(rows,index) { return rows[index].id; }
function archiveSelected(rows,selection,archive) { archive(selection); }
brief.after:
function select(rows,index) { return index; }
function archiveSelected(rows,selection,archive) { archive(rows[selection].id); }

expected.criterion: Storing a selected row index instead of its stable identity causes archive to target a different row after filtering or sorting changes the list order.

raw.title: Selection changes when rows are filtered or reordered
raw.evidence: select now stores the row index. Filtering or sorting replaces rows while preserving that index, so archiveSelected resolves it against a different row. This can archive the wrong row or throw if the index is out of range, violating the requirement to archive the row the user selected.

raw.title: Archive can target a different row after filtering or sorting
raw.evidence: Selection now stores a row index, while filtering and sorting replace `rows` without updating selection. `archiveSelected` looks up that index in the new array, so it can pass a different row's id to the persistence callback; if the index is out of range, the lookup fails.

triage.title: Archive loses the selected row after filtering or reordering
triage.evidence: select now stores an index instead of the immutable row id. Filter and sort replace rows while preserving selection, so archiveSelected can pass another row's id to archive or throw when the index is out of range. This violates the requirement to archive the originally selected row. Merged duplicate reports from Staff engineer and Product.

raw.title: Preserve the selected row’s immutable ID
raw.evidence: Selection now stores an index while filter and sort preserve selection but replace rows. Selecting A at index 0 in [A,B], then sorting to [B,A], causes archiveSelected to call archive(B.id), violating the requirement to archive A. Filtering can also leave the index out of bounds, causing rows[selection].id to throw.

raw.title: Selection no longer identifies the user's chosen row
raw.evidence: select now stores an index, which archiveSelected resolves against the current rows. Selecting A at index 0 and then reordering [A, B] to [B, A] archives B. Filtering can likewise target another row or leave the index out of bounds, causing an exception. This violates the requirement to archive the selected row after filtering or reordering. Preserve the immutable row ID as the selection.

triage.title: Preserve the selected row’s immutable ID
triage.evidence: Staff engineer and Product reports identify the same defect: select now stores an index, but filtering and sorting replace rows while preserving selection. Selecting A at index 0 in [A,B], then reordering to [B,A], makes archiveSelected call archive(B.id), violating the spec. Filtering can also leave the stored index out of bounds, causing rows[selection].id to throw.

raw.title: Selection stored as positional index; archive acts on wrong row after filter/sort
raw.evidence: select now returns the index, which is stored in parent state. Per context, filter and sort replace the rows but preserve the selection. archiveSelected then resolves rows[selection].id against the new row array, so the same index points to a different row. This violates the spec that archive must act on the user-selected row after filtering or reordering. The result is archiving of the wrong record. If the filtered list is shorter, rows[selection] is undefined and the call throws a TypeError. The before code stored the immutable unique id, which was stable across filter and sort.

raw.title: No guard for out-of-range or stale selection
raw.evidence: archiveSelected dereferences rows[selection].id without checking that the row exists. An empty list, a filtered list, or a null selection throws instead of being a safe no-op.

raw.title: No tests for the new behavior
raw.evidence: No tests are supplied. The spec's key scenarios (archive after filter, archive after sort, stale selection) are uncovered. A test that selects a row, reorders the rows, and archives would have caught the regression.

raw.title: Archive can act on the wrong row after filter or sort
raw.evidence: The spec requires archive to act on the row the user selected, even after the list is filtered or reordered. Selection is now stored as an index. Filter and sort replace the rows but keep the selection. So `rows[selection]` resolves against the new row order and can return a different row than the user chose. `archive` is the persistence callback, so it would archive the wrong record. If the filtered list is shorter, `rows[selection]` is undefined and `.id` throws. The old code kept the immutable unique id as the selection, which met the spec.

triage.title: Selection stored as a positional index, so archive hits the wrong row after filter or sort
triage.evidence: Both the Staff engineer and Product reports found this; they are merged here. Before the change, select returned rows[index].id. The context says that id is immutable and unique, so it stays valid when the list changes. After the change, select returns the index, which is kept in parent state. The context says filter and sort replace rows but keep the selection. archiveSelected then looks up rows[selection].id in the new array, so the same index can point to a different row. archive is the persistence callback, so this saves an archive of the wrong record. That breaks the spec requirement that archive act on the row the user selected after filtering or reordering. brief.context: quote returns either null or a nonnegative integer number of cents. The UI disables Continue unless available is true, and uses the returned cents in its order summary.

brief.spec: The search screen must display results for the most recently entered query. Older in-flight responses may arrive after newer ones.
brief.context: The input handler calls search for every query. fetchResults calls its callback exactly once and does not guarantee callback order. state is shared across calls.

expected.criterion: An older response can overwrite the latest query results because the request identity guard was removed; retain ordering protection or cancel obsolete requests.

raw.title: Stale-response guard removed: older responses can overwrite results for the newest query
raw.evidence: The before version saved `const request=++state.request` and the callback returned early when `request!==state.request`, so only the latest request could write `state.items`. The after version still increments `state.request` but never captures or compares it, and the callback assigns `state.items=items` unconditionally. The context says fetchResults does not guarantee callback order. So if a user types 'a' and then 'ab', and the 'a' response arrives last, the screen shows results for 'a'. This breaks the spec: 'must display results for the most recently entered query. Older in-flight responses may arrive after newer ones.'

raw.title: Unused request counter is left in place
raw.evidence: `++state.request` still runs, but nothing reads its value anymore. This makes it look like requests are still ordered when they aren't. Either restore the comparison (the correct fix) or remove the counter.

raw.title: Stale-response guard removed: older search results can overwrite newer ones
raw.evidence: Before, the code saved `const request=++state.request` and the callback checked `if(request!==state.request) return;` before writing results. After, the code still runs `++state.request`, but the callback does `state.items=items;` with no check. The context says fetchResults does not guarantee callback order, and the spec says older in-flight responses may arrive after newer ones. So a slow response for an earlier query can replace the results for the latest query. The user then sees results that don't match what they typed, which breaks the spec requirement to display results for the most recently entered query.

brief.spec: Report whether a resolved destination lies at or beneath the source root. Sibling paths that merely share the root prefix are allowed.
brief.context: The caller resolves symlinks before calling inside. Inputs are absolute POSIX paths, have no trailing slash, and have no dot segments. The root is always /repo.
brief.before: function inside(path) { return path==='/repo' || path.startsWith('/repo/'); }

raw.title: Rewrite adds no behavior and no regression tests for the sibling-prefix case
raw.evidence: Under the stated constraints (absolute POSIX path, no trailing slash, no dot segments, root always /repo), `parts[1]==='repo'` gives the same result as the old check. It is true for /repo and /repo/x. It is false for siblings such as /repo-evil and /repo2, and for /other/repo. The rewrite allocates an array to do what the old `===` / `startsWith('/repo/')` check did directly. It is also less obviously tied to the spec, because it compares only the first segment and not the full root. If the root became multi-segment, such as /a/repo, it would silently be wrong. No tests are included for the boundary cases that matter: /repo, /repo/x, /repo-evil, /repo2/x, and /other/repo.

raw.title: Rewrite is behaviorally equivalent but adds no value and has no tests
raw.evidence: Under the stated input constraints (absolute POSIX path, no trailing slash, no dot segments, root always /repo), `parts[1]==='repo'` gives the same result as the old check. '/repo' and '/repo/x' return true. '/repo-sibling' and '/other/repo' return false. The new form allocates an array for every call. It also hides the 'at or beneath /repo' intent, because the root is encoded only as a segment index. It is more fragile if the root ever changes to a multi-segment path or if the input contract loosens. No tests cover the sibling-prefix case (/repo-x), the exact root, or nested paths.

notes: Raw finding 0 acknowledges behavioral equivalence under the supplied contract. Allocation, readability, hypothetical root changes, and missing tests identify no expected defect; pending human adjudication.
